verdict.reasoning: Patient states wheeze started about two days ago: “it started, like, about two days ago.”
Patient links onset to cleaning and dust and timing: “it started, like, about two days ago… I was, like, cleaning the house… all this dust came out… it started after maybe, uh, an hour or so.”
Worsening at night and shortness of breath are both described: “it get's a bit worse, um, at night, I find” and “I'm feeling like a little bit, uh, uh, short of breath.”
Patient notes difficulty completing sentences: “when I'm… talking… I start finding that, uh, sometimes, um, I'm unable to , complete my sentences.”
Patient denies pain with deep breath and dizziness: “Mmm, no, no. No pain.” and “no. No dizziness. Uh, none of that.” This supports no pleuritic chest pain or dizziness.
Oral intake and water intake documented: “have you been eating and drinking OK…?” / “Yeah… I think I'm having, like, you know, four or five glasses a day.”
No meds taken for this episode: “have you taken anything for the wheeze?” / “Uh, no. No, I haven't actually.”
History of childhood asthma: “I used to have, like, a bit of, um, asthma, uh, as a child.”
History of hay fever: “also in the summer I sometimes get, um, hay fever.”
Patient describes asthma triggered by running: “sometimes when I, um, run for, like, long periods, it can, it can start up a bit.” This is consistent with exercise‑induced bronchospasm.

Patient has an asthma inhaler from a few months ago: “I have, uh, I have, like, an asthma inhaler. I use that.” and later “I think I might have one from, like, a couple of months ago.” A short‑acting bronchodilator inhaler (SABA) is the standard context.
Prior steroid courses for asthma: “I have, before, taken steroids for asthma.”
No known allergies documented: “And, apart from this, do you know if you're allergic to anything?” / “Uh, not that I know of.”
Patient is a short drive from GP surgery: “How far are you away from a doctor's surgery…?” / “Uh, they may be minutes' drive away.” Living “near” the surgery is a reasonable inference.
All elements appear: wheeze and SOB for about 2 days after dust exposure and history of childhood asthma and hay fever are all described in the transcript as above.
Doctor frames differential as asthma vs allergy: “This could be one of two things. But, we want to rule out asthma or an allergy first.”

In‑person evaluation with pulse oximetry and to determine need for steroids: “you'll need… visit one of our clinics… so we can do some more tests… use a small device on your finger, to check the amount of oxygen in your blood… from that we can tell if it's asthma or something else” and “you may need to take some steroids now. But… we won't be able to know until we've done those tests first.”

OTC antihistamine trial and GP prescription if not available: “if you've got something, like an antihistamine… I would take one” and when patient says she has none, doctor says, “You might be able to get one on your way to the doctor's surgery. If not, they can prescribe you one.”
Letter via app for GP: “I'm gonna write a letter for your GP, just to let him know what's happened… You should get the letter over the app. And then… you can take yourself to the GP.”
Duration of in‑person visit discussed: “the consultation with the GP in person shouldn't take too long.” / Patient: “How long do you think it will take?” / Doctor: “Probably ten minutes.”
